child_drafts.description_long: At a May 14, 2026 House education committee hearing, Education Secretary Linda McMahon defended the administration’s effort to wind down the Department of Education. KPBS, reporting on NPR material and citing Office of Personnel Management data, said department staffing had declined from roughly 4,200 employees in 2024 to about 2,300 in 2026, or approximately 45%. The same report said more than 100 programs and obligations had shifted to other agencies. Examples included elementary and secondary education functions moving to the Department of Labor and family-engagement work moving to Health and Human Services. The staffing figures were reported as OPM data and describe the department’s workforce across the period, not a single reduction on the hearing date. McMahon testified before a House education committee while defending the administration’s effort to wind down the department. The article also discussed potential future transfers and the proposed FY2027 budget, but the reported staffing total and completed program shifts are the discrete facts attached to this event.

child_drafts.title: Education Department Announces Six Interagency Agreements
child_drafts.description_short: ED announced six agreements with Labor, Interior, HHS and State to share administration of federal education programs, while retaining policy and award authority, according to CRS.
child_drafts.description_medium: The Congressional Research Service says the six agreements announced November 18, 2025 direct partner agencies to perform administrative tasks supporting Education Department programs. ED transfers funds for those services but retains budget formulation, policy clearance, annual grant awards and program accountability. The agreements’ legal basis is contested; CRS describes the legality as unresolved.
child_drafts.description_long: On November 18, 2025, the Education Department announced six interagency agreements with Labor, Interior, Health and Human Services, and State. The Congressional Research Service reviewed the agreements and says partner agencies were assigned administrative tasks supporting ED programs, while ED retained budget formulation, policy clearance, annual grant awards and program accountability. Under the agreements, ED transfers funds for partner agencies’ services. CRS notes that Title I-A grants total about $18.4 billion annually and that the agreements span services for federal programs, but they do not transfer ED’s statutory functions wholesale. ED appears to rely primarily on the Economy Act, 31 U.S.C. § 1535, which permits agencies to obtain services from one another. The legality of using that authority for these arrangements has been challenged and remained unresolved in the CRS account. The agreements therefore document a dated administrative arrangement; they do not establish that the department had already been abolished or that all education programs had moved.

child_drafts.description_long: President Donald Trump signed the Rescissions Act of 2025 on July 24, 2025. The enacted statute states that the rescissions in the act took effect upon enactment. Section 2(b)(20) rescinded amounts made available to the Corporation for Public Broadcasting for fiscal years 2026 and 2027, including amounts provided through the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2024 and the Full-Year Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2025. This is a specific statutory cancellation of future CPB appropriations. The law text does not say that $1.1 billion was cut, and it does not quantify how individual public television or radio stations would be affected. Those amounts and downstream effects require separate appropriations records or station-level evidence. The underlying congressional action is distinct from the separate settlement of Trump’s 60 Minutes lawsuit and the later White House media-bias webpage. The statutory text supports the date, effective timing and fiscal-year scope of the CPB rescission; it does not establish the broader claim that all public broadcasting was immediately defunded.

child_drafts.title: Trump asks DOJ to investigate Epstein ties of Clinton and other political targets
child_drafts.description_short: Trump said he would ask the Justice Department to investigate Jeffrey Epstein's ties to Bill Clinton, JPMorgan and others.
child_drafts.description_medium: On November 14, 2025, Trump asked DOJ to investigate Epstein-related ties of Bill Clinton, Larry Summers, Reid Hoffman and JPMorgan; DOJ said it would comply and assigned Jay Clayton. Reuters said no credible evidence linked the named individuals to Epstein’s trafficking. Reuters said the request followed House Oversight’s release of Epstein documents.
child_drafts.description_long: On November 14, 2025, President Trump publicly asked the Justice Department to investigate Jeffrey Epstein’s connections with former President Bill Clinton, former Treasury Secretary Larry Summers, investor Reid Hoffman and JPMorgan. Reuters reported that Attorney General Pam Bondi said Manhattan U.S. Attorney Jay Clayton would lead the investigation. The request came two days after the House Oversight Committee released a large set of Epstein-related documents and amid renewed political attention to Trump’s own past association with Epstein. Reuters reported that no credible evidence had surfaced linking Clinton, Summers or Hoffman to Epstein’s sex trafficking; the named individuals denied wrongdoing or described their contacts. This entry should report the request and DOJ’s stated response without suggesting that the investigation found crimes or that the targets had been accused of sexual offenses. It is separate from the July DOJ/FBI memorandum and the July defamation lawsuit over the birthday-note story.
